title: Number of Good Pairs
statement: Call a pair of indices `(i, j)` of the integer array `nums` good when `i < j` and the two positions hold the same value, `nums[i] == nums[j]`. Count the good pairs and return that count.
notes:
## Intuition

Comparing every pair of indices works but costs O(n²). Look at it from the right end of each pair instead: when index `j` holds value `v`, it forms a good pair with every earlier index that also holds `v`. So if we keep a running count of how many times each value has appeared, each element adds exactly that count to the answer. (Equivalently, a value that appears `c` times contributes `c · (c − 1) / 2` pairs.)

## Approach

1. Keep a map `count` from each value to how often it has appeared so far, and a total `pairs`.
2. For each `value` in `nums`, read `seen`, its count so far.
3. Add `seen` to `pairs`: the current index closes one good pair with each earlier copy.
4. Store `seen + 1` as the new count, then return `pairs` at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3]`. The first three values are new, so each adds 0. The second `1` sees one earlier `1` (`pairs = 1`), the third `1` sees two (`pairs = 3`), and the second `3` sees one (`pairs = 4`). The answer is `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant-time map operations.
- Space: O(m) for the map, where m is the number of distinct values (at most 100).

## Pitfalls

- Add the count **before** incrementing it, or every element pairs with itself.
- Pairs are unordered with `i < j`; counting `(i, j)` and `(j, i)` both would double the answer.
- A value seen once contributes nothing; do not add 1 for it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | how many times each value has appeared so far |
| `pairs` | good pairs found so far |
| `value` | the current element |
| `seen` | earlier copies of `value`, i.e. new pairs it closes |

narration.2: Start an empty tally of how often each value has appeared.
narration.3: No good pairs have been found yet.
narration.4: Visit the elements from left to right; each one is the right end of its pairs.
narration.5: Look up how many earlier elements had this same value.
narration.6: Each earlier copy forms one good pair with the current element.
narration.7: Count the current element so later copies can pair with it.
narration.9: Every pair was counted exactly once, at its right end.
